```{r helpers, echo=FALSE}
draw_workflow <- function(highlight = NULL, cex = 0.9) {
  boxes <- c("PROBLEM", "THEORIES", "MODELS", "FIT", "COMPARE")
  subs <- c("what do we\nneed to know?", "candidate\nexplanations",
            "data-generating\n(process + noise)", "confront each\nwith data",
            "fit, prediction,\nrelevance")
  x <- seq(1, 9, by = 2)
  y <- 2
  w <- 0.8
  h <- 0.55
  shade <- function(lab) if (!is.null(highlight) && lab %in% highlight) "lightskyblue1" else "white"
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(-0.2, 4), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_along(boxes)) {
    rect(x[i] - w, y - h, x[i] + w, y + h, col = shade(boxes[i]), lwd = 1.5)
    text(x[i], y + 0.18, boxes[i], font = 2, cex = cex)
    text(x[i], y - 0.22, subs[i], cex = cex * 0.75)
  }
  arrows(x[-5] + w, y, x[-1] - w, y, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  rect(6 - 0.7, 3.2 - 0.35, 6 + 0.7, 3.2 + 0.35, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 3.28, "DATA", font = 2, cex = cex)
  text(6, 3.0, "study design", cex = cex * 0.75)
  arrows(x[3], y + h, 6 - 0.7, 3.2, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  arrows(6 + 0.7, 3.2, x[4], y + h, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  segments(x[5], y - h, x[5], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  segments(x[5], 0.4, x[1], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  arrows(x[c(1, 2)], 0.4, x[c(1, 2)], y - h, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 0.15, "REVISE the problem and theories; drop or down-weight poor models",
       cex = cex * 0.85, font = 3)
}
```

[How this page was made](#ai-use)

This page has no companion script and no assigned reading. It is a
short review of the course followed by a guide to what to learn next,
with resources for each topic. Most of the books linked here are free
online; where a book is not, the link goes to the publisher's page.

# Review and where to go next {#next}

This course taught one skill: writing down a model of how your data
came to be, and fitting it. The first part of this page maps the
semester onto the modeling workflow. The rest suggests where to go
from here: the habits that carry a course skill into a real analysis,
the math worth strengthening, causal inference, hierarchical Bayesian
models, and machine learning for prediction.

## 1. What the course covered {#review}

```{r workflow, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3, dev="png", dpi=250}
draw_workflow()
```

Every model this semester had the same parts: a deterministic
function for the signal, a probability distribution for the noise,
and a likelihood that connects the two to data. What changed from
week to week was how elaborate the parts were and how the fitting was
done. The table lists the weeks by the workflow box they belong to.

| Workflow box | What you can now do | Where |
|:-------------|:--------------------------------------------|:-----------------|
| PROBLEM, THEORIES | Start from the question; write rival explanations as rival models | [Week 1](Week1_IntroAndAlgorithms.html) |
| MODELS | Choose a deterministic function from the bestiary and a distribution for the noise; simulate data from the result | [Week 2](Week2_DeterministicFunctions.html), [Week 3](Week3_ProbabilityAndBayes.html), [Week 4](Week4_ProbabilityDistributions.html), [Week 5](Week5_SimulatingData.html) |
| DATA | Use simulation to ask whether a study design can answer the question | [Week 6](Week6_LikelihoodAndPowerAnalysis.html#power) |
| FIT | Write a likelihood and maximize it; put intervals on the estimates; combine a likelihood with a prior and sample the posterior | [Week 6](Week6_LikelihoodAndPowerAnalysis.html), [Week 7](Week7_IntervalsAndBayes.html), [Week 8](Week8_PosteriorsAndOptimization.html), [Week 9](Week9_MCMC.html) |
| COMPARE | Check goodness of fit; compare models by likelihood ratio, AIC, and cross-validation; shrink coefficients with a penalty | [Week 10](Week10_ModelComparison.html), [model performance](Bonus_ModelPerformance.html) |
| MODELS and FIT, for data that are not independent | Model the variance as well as the mean: random effects, autocorrelation, hierarchical models, smooths, spatial fields, hidden states | [Week 11](Week11_LinearModelsAndVariance.html), [Week 12](Week12_MixedModels.html), [Week 13](Week13_HierarchicalModelsAndGAMs.html), [Week 14](Week14_SpatialRegression.html), [Week 15](Week15_DynamicModels.html) |

Two ideas ran through the second half of the course and are worth
keeping in view as you read the rest of this page.

**Dependence goes in the model.** Trees in one stand, years in one
series, and plots near each other on a map share something the
covariates do not explain. A random effect, an AR(1) term, a smooth,
and a spatial field are all ways of writing that shared part down,
and all of them amount to a multivariate normal with a structured
covariance matrix.

**A penalty is a prior.** Ridge and lasso penalties, the variance of
a random effect, and the wiggliness penalty on a spline all pull
estimates toward something simpler, by an amount the data help
choose. Most of the methods in sections [5](#bayes) and [6](#ml) are
variations on this.

> **Question:** Pick one analysis from your thesis or project. Which
> workflow box did you spend the least time on, and what would it
> have changed if you had spent more?

```{asis, echo=FALSE}
*Land:* No single answer. Most students name PROBLEM/THEORIES (they
started from the data) or COMPARE (fit one model and stopped). Use
whichever comes up to motivate section 2.
```

## 2. From coursework to a real analysis {#practice}

Real data sets are messier than the ones on these pages, most of
which were simulated so that the truth was known. A few habits matter
more than any new method.

**Decide what the model is for.** The same data can serve three
different goals, and they call for different tools and different
checks.^[Shmueli (2010,
["To explain or to predict?"](https://doi.org/10.1214/10-STS330)
*Statistical Science* 25: 289-310) is the standard reference for the
first two rows. Breiman (2001,
["Statistical modeling: the two cultures"](https://doi.org/10.1214/ss/1009213726)
*Statistical Science* 16: 199-231) argues, with some heat, that
statisticians had neglected prediction.]

| Goal | The question | What counts as success | Where to look |
|:-----|:--------------------------|:--------------------------|:--------------|
| Explain | What would happen to $y$ if we changed $x$? | An effect estimate you can defend against confounding | [Causal inference](#causal) |
| Predict | What will $y$ be at new sites or times? | Low error on data the model has not seen | [Machine learning](#ml) |
| Decide | Which action best meets the objectives? | A choice that holds up across what you don't know | Decision analysis (below) |

A model built for one goal can be poor at another. The model with the
best AIC can give a badly biased effect estimate (see the
[causal diagrams](Week10_ModelComparison.html#dags) section of the
Week 10 page), and a model with a well-identified effect can predict
poorly.

**Simulate before you fit.** Before trusting a new model on real
data, simulate data from it with known parameter values and check
that your code recovers them. Every worked example in this course did
this. It catches coding errors, shows which parameters the design can
estimate, and tells you how much data you need.

**Build up from a simple model.** Fit the simplest version first,
check it, and add one piece at a time. When a complicated model fails
to converge, the last model that worked tells you where to
look.^[Gelman et al. (2020,
["Bayesian workflow"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.01808), arXiv
2011.01808) lays out this way of working at length: prior predictive
checks, fitting to simulated data, building models up in steps, and
what to do when computation fails. Most of it applies to maximum
likelihood too. For presenting a regression-type analysis, see Zuur
and Ieno (2016,
["A protocol for conducting and presenting results of regression-type analyses"](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12577),
*Methods in Ecology and Evolution* 7: 636-645).]

**Check the fit against the data, every time.** Simulate from the
fitted model and compare with what you observed, using residuals, a
variogram, an ACF, or a posterior predictive check as the data
require. A model that wins a comparison can still fit badly.

**Make the analysis reproducible.** Raw data are never edited by
hand, every figure and number comes from a script, and the project
is under version control.^[Wilson et al. (2017,
["Good enough practices in scientific computing"](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005510),
*PLOS Computational Biology* 13: e1005510) is a short, practical
list. [*R for Data Science*](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) (Wickham,
Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Grolemund; free online) covers the data
wrangling this course mostly skipped.]

**For management questions, carry the uncertainty through to the
decision.** A manager rarely needs a p-value. They need to know what
is likely to happen under each option and how sure you are.
Structured decision making is the framework for this, and ecological
forecasting treats prediction as something to be scored and improved
over time.^[Conroy and Peterson (2013,
[*Decision Making in Natural Resource Management*](https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118506196),
Wiley) covers structured and adaptive decision making. Dietze (2017,
[*Ecological Forecasting*](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400885459),
Princeton University Press) builds on state-space models like those
on the [Week 15 page](Week15_DynamicModels.html#state-space); the
[Ecological Forecasting Initiative](https://ecoforecast.org/) runs
forecasting challenges and posts teaching material.]

## 3. Mathematical tools {#math}

The course kept the math to what a second semester of calculus and
one statistics course supply. More math does not make someone a
better ecologist, but four areas pay back the time quickly, because
they are what the papers and software manuals are written in.

| Tool | Where it appeared here | What more of it buys you | Where to learn it |
|:-----|:------------------|:----------------------|:--------------------------|
| Linear algebra | Design matrices, covariance matrices, $V = ZGZ^T + \sigma_e^2 R$ ([Week 11](Week11_LinearModelsAndVariance.html#linear-algebra)) | Reading any mixed, spatial, or multivariate model; knowing why a fit is slow or singular; eigenvalues for stability and ordination | [3Blue1Brown, *Essence of Linear Algebra*](https://www.3blue1brown.com/topics/linear-algebra) (videos, for the geometry); [Strang's MIT course 18.06](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/) (free lectures and problems) |
| Calculus and optimization | Derivatives for maxima, Newton's method, the Hessian, integrals over densities | Understanding gradients (what Stan, `TMB`, and neural networks all compute), the Laplace approximation, and why reparameterizing helps | [3Blue1Brown, *Essence of Calculus*](https://www.3blue1brown.com/topics/calculus); Deisenroth, Faisal, and Ong, [*Mathematics for Machine Learning*](https://mml-book.github.io/) (free; chapters 2-7 cover linear algebra, vector calculus, probability, and optimization at about the right level) |
| Probability | Distributions, expectation, conditional probability, Bayes' rule | Deriving a likelihood for a new sampling design; marginalizing over hidden states; reading a hierarchical model | Blitzstein and Hwang, [*Introduction to Probability*](https://doi.org/10.1201/9780429428357) (the book and the Harvard Stat 110 lectures are free online) |
| Differential equations | The logistic curve from a growth rate ([Week 2](Week2_DeterministicFunctions.html#mechanism)); dynamic models ([Week 15](Week15_DynamicModels.html)) | Building a mechanistic model from rates (growth, transmission, uptake) and fitting it to data instead of choosing a curve by its shape | Otto and Day, [*A Biologist's Guide to Mathematical Modeling in Ecology and Evolution*](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400840915); [3Blue1Brown on differential equations](https://www.3blue1brown.com/topics/differential-equations); Strogatz, [*Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos*](https://doi.org/10.1201/9780429492563) |

If you pick one, pick linear algebra. Every model from Week 11 on
was a statement about a mean vector and a covariance matrix, and the
documentation for `glmmTMB`, `mgcv`, `INLA`, and Stan assumes you can
read one.

Differential equations are the natural next step for anyone whose
question is about a process through time (population dynamics,
disease, nutrient cycling, hydrology). In R, the
[`deSolve`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=deSolve) package
solves a system of differential equations numerically, and the
solution can serve as the deterministic part of a likelihood, just
as a bestiary function did. Stan has built-in solvers for the same
purpose.^[Otto and Day is the friendliest way in for biologists: it
starts from how to turn a verbal description into equations and
teaches the math (equilibria, stability, matrices) as each model
needs it. See the "Ordinary Differential Equations" chapter of the
[Stan User's Guide](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/) for
fitting.]

Watching lectures is not enough for any of these. Work problems by
hand, and when a paper gives a model in matrix form, write out the
matrices for a toy case with three observations.

## 4. Causal inference {#causal}

Most questions in ecology and management are causal. Does grazing
reduce sage-grouse nest success? Did the restoration raise the water
table? Would closing the road help? A regression coefficient answers
a different question (how does $y$ differ, on average, between units
that differ in $x$, holding the other covariates in the model
fixed?), and the two agree only under assumptions about how the data
came to be.

The [Week 10 page](Week10_ModelComparison.html#dags) introduced
causal diagrams (DAGs) and showed that the choice of covariates
depends on the diagram, not on AIC: adjusting for a confounder
removes bias, adjusting for a mediator hides part of the effect, and
adjusting for a collider creates an association where none exists.
Causal inference is the set of tools for making those assumptions
explicit and for designing analyses around them.

| Approach | The idea | An example |
|:---------|:------------------------------|:------------------------------|
| Randomized experiment | Random assignment breaks every arrow into the treatment | Grazing exclosures assigned to plots by coin flip |
| Adjustment from a DAG | Draw the diagram, find a set of covariates that blocks the back-door paths, and condition on it | Effect of fire on cheatgrass, adjusting for elevation and prior cover |
| Matching and weighting | Compare treated units with untreated units that had a similar chance of being treated | Protected vs. unprotected parcels matched on slope, access, and land value |
| Before-after-control-impact, difference-in-differences | Use the change at control sites as the change the treated sites would have shown without treatment | Stream temperature before and after riparian planting, against unplanted reaches |
| Instrumental variables | Find a variable that moves the treatment but touches the outcome by no other route | Distance to a hatchery as a source of variation in stocking |
| Regression discontinuity | Compare units just on either side of an arbitrary cutoff | Parcels just inside and just outside a reserve boundary |
| Structural equation models | Fit the whole diagram, direct and indirect paths together | Precipitation affects grouse through forb cover and through insects |

None of these removes the need for judgment. Each trades one
untestable assumption (no unmeasured confounding) for another
(parallel trends, a valid instrument), and the diagram is where the
assumptions get written down so that others can argue with them.

**Where to learn more:**

- McElreath, [*Statistical Rethinking*](https://doi.org/10.1201/9780429029608)
  (2nd ed., 2020), and his free
  [lecture series](https://github.com/rmcelreath/stat_rethinking_2026).
  It teaches Bayesian modeling and causal diagrams together, in R,
  with ecological examples. If you read one book after this course,
  this is a good candidate.
- Pearl and Mackenzie, *The Book of Why* (2018). No math; the history
  and the ideas.
- Hernán and Robins,
  [*Causal Inference: What If*](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook)
  (free online). The careful version, from epidemiology.
- Huntington-Klein, [*The Effect*](https://theeffectbook.net/), and
  Cunningham,
  [*Causal Inference: The Mixtape*](https://mixtape.scunning.com/)
  (both free online). The quasi-experimental designs in the table,
  with R code.
- Shipley,
  [*Cause and Correlation in Biology*](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139979573)
  (2nd ed., 2016), for path analysis and structural equation models.
- For ecology: Larsen, Meng, and Kendall (2019,
  ["Causal analysis in control-impact ecological studies with observational data"](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13190),
  *Methods in Ecology and Evolution* 10: 924-934); Arif and MacNeil
  (2023,
  ["Applying the structural causal model framework for observational causal inference in ecology"](https://doi.org/10.1002/ecm.1554),
  *Ecological Monographs* 93: e1554); Siegel and Dee (2025,
  ["Foundations and future directions for causal inference in ecological research"](https://doi.org/10.1111/ele.70053),
  *Ecology Letters* 28: e70053).
- [DAGitty](https://dagitty.net/) draws a diagram in the browser and
  lists the adjustment sets it implies.

**At UNR:** NRES 701A, *Causal Inference and Analysis* (Spring 2027,
2 credits, Kevin Shoemaker and Todd Steury), covers causal diagrams,
experiments and quasi-experiments, structural equation models, and
time-series approaches, with a project in which each student builds
a causal diagram for their own study system. See the
[draft course website](https://kevintshoemaker.github.io/Causal-Inference/).

> **Question:** A survey of 80 meadows finds willow cover 30% higher
> where beavers are present, and the beaver term lowers AIC by 14.
> A colleague wants to report that reintroducing beavers will raise
> willow cover by 30%. What would you need to know before agreeing?

```{asis, echo=FALSE}
*Land:* Which way the arrow runs (beavers settle where willow is
already dense: reverse causation) and what drives both (water table,
stream gradient, grazing pressure: confounders). AIC says the term
predicts; it says nothing about what an intervention would do. A
design answer: willow before and after reintroduction at treated and
untreated meadows (BACI).
```

## 5. Hierarchical Bayesian models {#bayes}

The [Week 13 page](Week13_HierarchicalModelsAndGAMs.html#bayesian-hierarchical)
fit one hierarchical model in Stan and `brms`. That is enough to
read the literature, and a start on writing your own. Ecological
data are a natural fit for this kind of model because they are
usually observed imperfectly, grouped (sites, years, individuals,
species), and unbalanced. A hierarchical model lets you write a
separate piece for the ecological process and for how it was
observed, and it carries the uncertainty from each piece into the
final answer.

The [state-space models](Week15_DynamicModels.html#state-space) of
Week 15 have this structure already: a process equation for the
hidden population state, an observation equation for the counts, and
parameters above both. That page fit them by maximum likelihood, with
the Kalman filter and with `RTMB`. A Bayesian fit treats each year's
hidden state as one more unknown to sample, which makes it
straightforward to go beyond what the Kalman filter can handle:
non-normal counts, nonlinear dynamics, several populations sharing
parameters, or prior information on the process and observation
variances, which the data alone often cannot
separate.^[The Week 15 page showed how often maximum likelihood puts
one of the two variances at zero in a short series
([what goes wrong](Week15_DynamicModels.html#identifiability)). A
prior on the observation SD, taken from repeat counts or a
double-observer study, is the usual remedy. Auger-Méthé et al.
(2021,
["A guide to state-space modeling of ecological time series"](https://doi.org/10.1002/ecm.1470),
*Ecological Monographs* 91: e01470) covers both frequentist and
Bayesian fitting, with code.]

### When a Bayesian fit is worth it {#bayes-when}

For a standard mixed model with plenty of groups, `glmmTMB` and
`brms` give nearly the same answer and `glmmTMB` is faster. The
Bayesian version earns its extra computing time when:

- **there are few groups**, so a variance component is poorly
  estimated and maximum likelihood puts it at zero or returns a
  singular fit (a weakly informative prior keeps it away from the
  boundary);
- **you have real prior information**, such as a survival rate from
  earlier studies of the species;
- **the quantity you care about is derived** from several parameters
  (a population growth rate, the probability that a trend is below
  a threshold, a difference between two predicted values), since
  posterior draws give its uncertainty with one line of code;
- **the model has latent states or missing data**, as in occupancy,
  capture-recapture, and state-space models;
- **you are combining data sources** that inform the same process
  (counts and telemetry, say) in one model.

### Which software {#bayes-software}

| Tool | What it is | Use it when | Limits |
|:-----|:--------------------------|:--------------------------|:--------------------------|
| [`brms`](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/) | Formula interface (`lme4` syntax) that writes and runs a Stan program | The model is a regression with random effects, smooths, or common correlation structures. Start here. | Models that don't fit a formula (custom likelihoods can be added, with effort) |
| [Stan](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/) | A language for writing any model with a differentiable log posterior; Hamiltonian Monte Carlo | You need a model no package offers: a custom process model, a differential equation, an unusual observation process | No discrete parameters, so latent discrete states have to be summed out by hand (as the [Week 15 page](Week15_DynamicModels.html#forward) did for occupancy) |
| [NIMBLE](https://r-nimble.org/) and JAGS | The BUGS modeling language; Gibbs and Metropolis samplers | Models with discrete latent states written directly: occupancy, N-mixture, capture-recapture, integrated population models. Most wildlife population books use this language. | Can mix slowly when parameters are strongly correlated |
| [`INLA`](https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/) and [`inlabru`](https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/) | A fast approximation to the posterior, with no sampling, for models whose latent part is Gaussian | Large spatial and spatiotemporal models ([Week 14](Week14_SpatialRegression.html#packages)), where MCMC would take days | Restricted to latent Gaussian models; the approximation is hard to check from the inside |
| `glmmTMB`, `sdmTMB`, [`RTMB`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=RTMB) | Maximum likelihood with the random effects integrated out by the Laplace approximation | Speed matters and priors don't; model comparison across many candidates; very large data sets | Not Bayesian by default; intervals lean on a normal approximation |

A reasonable path: fit with `glmmTMB` or `sdmTMB` while you are
still choosing the model's structure, move to `brms` when you need
posterior draws or priors, and write Stan (or NIMBLE) yourself only
when no package fits the model. `brms` will show you the Stan
program it wrote (`stancode()`), which is a good way to learn the
language.

### Where to learn more {#bayes-resources}

- Hobbs and Hooten,
  [*Bayesian Models: A Statistical Primer for Ecologists*](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400866557)
  (2015). Short, and written for this audience: how to write a
  hierarchical model down correctly before touching software.
- McElreath, [*Statistical Rethinking*](https://doi.org/10.1201/9780429029608),
  again.
- Gelman, Hill, and Vehtari,
  [*Regression and Other Stories*](https://avehtari.github.io/ROS-Examples/)
  (free online), for applied regression done the Bayesian way; and
  Gelman et al.,
  [*Bayesian Data Analysis*](https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/book/)
  (3rd ed., free online), as the reference.
- The [Stan User's Guide](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/)
  and the Stan
  [case studies](https://mc-stan.org/learn-stan/case-studies.html).
  The [Stan forum](https://discourse.mc-stan.org/) answers `brms`
  questions too.
- Kéry and Royle,
  [*Applied Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology*](https://doi.org/10.1016/C2013-0-19160-X)
  (2016), for occupancy, abundance, and distribution models with
  imperfect detection.
- Hooten and Hefley,
  [*Bringing Bayesian Models to Life*](https://doi.org/10.1201/9780429243653)
  (2019), for writing your own MCMC samplers in R, one model at a
  time.
- For `INLA`: Gómez-Rubio,
  [*Bayesian Inference with INLA*](https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/),
  and Krainski et al.,
  [*Advanced Spatial Modeling with Stochastic Partial Differential Equations Using R and INLA*](https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/)
  (both free online).

**At UNR:** NRES 779, *Bayesian Hierarchical Modeling*, taught each
spring by Perry Williams, goes from probability rules to writing and
fitting your own hierarchical models. It is the direct follow-up to
the Bayesian weeks of this course.

## 6. Machine learning {#ml}

Everything so far in this course asked you to specify the model: you
chose the function and the distribution, and the parameters meant
something. Machine learning methods take the other route. They learn
a flexible function from the data, with the form left mostly open,
and they are judged by one thing: prediction error on data held out
from fitting.

You have already met the main ideas. Ridge and lasso
([Week 10](Week10_ModelComparison.html)) are machine learning
methods, and so is cross-validation as a way to set a penalty. A GAM
or a Gaussian process ([Week 13](Week13_HierarchicalModelsAndGAMs.html#gams))
learns the shape of a curve from the data. The
[random forest page](Bonus_RandomForest.html) works one method from
start to finish.

### When to reach for it {#ml-when}

Machine learning tends to beat a hand-specified model when there are
many predictors, the relationships are nonlinear with interactions
you could not list in advance, there is a lot of data, and the goal
is prediction: mapping habitat, classifying images or sounds,
filling gaps in a sensor record.

It is the wrong tool, or at least not enough alone, when you need an
effect estimate, when data are few, or when predictions must
extrapolate beyond the conditions sampled (a new climate, a
management action never tried). The costs to keep in mind:

- **Importance is not effect.** A variable-importance score says a
  predictor was useful for prediction given the others. It is not an
  estimate of what would happen if you changed that variable (see
  [section 4](#causal)).
- **Uncertainty is harder to get.** Most methods return a prediction
  with no interval, and the intervals that can be had usually ignore
  spatial or temporal dependence.
- **Validation has to respect the data's structure.** Random
  cross-validation folds flatter any flexible model when the data
  are clustered in space or time, as the
  [Week 14 demo](Week14_SpatialRegression.html#demo-compare)
  showed. Hold out whole blocks, sites, or years.^[Roberts et al.
  (2017,
  ["Cross-validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure"](https://doi.org/10.1111/ecog.02881),
  *Ecography* 40: 913-929).]
- **Flexible models need a lot of data** and are easy to overfit, so
  the tuning (tree depth, learning rate, penalty) matters as much as
  the choice of method.

### Common methods {#ml-methods}

| Method | How it works, briefly | Typical uses in ecology and environmental science | R packages |
|:-------|:--------------------------|:--------------------------|:-----------|
| Penalized regression (ridge, lasso, elastic net) | A linear model with a penalty on coefficient size | Many candidate covariates and modest sample sizes; a baseline for everything below | `glmnet` |
| GAMs and Gaussian processes | Smooth curves or surfaces with a wiggliness penalty | Nonlinear responses, spatial and seasonal smooths, with intervals; often competitive with the methods below on small data | `mgcv`, `brms` |
| Random forests | The average of many decision trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample | Species distribution and habitat models, land-cover classification, a first pass at which predictors matter | `ranger`, `randomForest` |
| Gradient boosted trees | Small trees added one at a time, each fit to the errors of those before | Usually the most accurate method for tabular data: distribution models, fire occurrence, water quality from catchment attributes | `xgboost`, `lightgbm`, `gbm` |
| MaxEnt | Penalized regression on presence-only records against background points (a Poisson point process model) | Distribution models from museum and citizen-science records with no absences | `maxnet`, `dismo` |
| Support vector machines | A boundary between classes with the widest margin, made nonlinear by a kernel | Classifying remote-sensing pixels; less used now than tree methods | `e1071`, `kernlab` |
| Neural networks (feed-forward) | Layers of weighted sums passed through nonlinear functions, trained by gradient descent | Large tabular or multi-species data sets (joint species distribution models, emulators of slow simulation models) | `torch`, `keras3`, `cito` |
| Convolutional networks and vision transformers | Neural networks built for images and spectrograms | Camera-trap species identification, bird and bat call classification, land cover and tree crowns from imagery | `torch`; usually pretrained models, often in Python |
| Recurrent networks and sequence transformers | Neural networks built for ordered data | Streamflow and water temperature forecasting, animal movement tracks, sensor gap-filling | `torch` |
| Unsupervised methods (clustering, ordination) | Find groups or gradients with no response variable | Community composition (NMDS, PCA), defining vegetation types, behavioral states from accelerometers | `vegan`, `cluster`, `mclust` |

Two practical notes. For tabular data (rows are sites, columns are
covariates), which is most of what ecologists have, start with a GAM
or a penalized regression as the baseline and then try a random
forest or boosted trees; deep learning rarely beats them
there.^[Elith, Leathwick, and Hastie (2008,
["A working guide to boosted regression trees"](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2656.2008.01390.x),
*Journal of Animal Ecology* 77: 802-813) is still the clearest
ecological introduction to boosting. For MaxEnt, see Elith et al.
(2011,
["A statistical explanation of MaxEnt for ecologists"](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1472-4642.2010.00725.x),
*Diversity and Distributions* 17: 43-57).] For images, audio, and
text, deep learning is the only serious option, and almost nobody
trains a network from scratch: you start from a model someone else
trained on millions of examples and adapt it to your data.

The line between the two approaches is also less sharp than it
looks. A neural network trained with weight decay is a model fit by
penalized maximum likelihood, and the penalty is a Normal prior on
the weights, the same result as the
[ridge prior](Week13_HierarchicalModelsAndGAMs.html#ridge-prior).
What differs is the number of parameters and the fact that they are
not meant to be interpreted.

### Where to learn more {#ml-resources}

- James, Witten, Hastie, and Tibshirani,
  [*An Introduction to Statistical Learning*](https://www.statlearning.com/)
  (2nd ed., free online, with R labs). The best starting point, at
  about the level of this course. Its longer and more mathematical
  parent is Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman,
  [*The Elements of Statistical Learning*](https://hastie.su.domains/ElemStatLearn/)
  (free online).
- Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville,
  [*Deep Learning*](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/) (2016, free
  online). The standard text on the theory. Part I is a compact
  review of the linear algebra, probability, and optimization it
  needs. It predates transformers, so pair it with something
  current, such as Zhang et al.,
  [*Dive into Deep Learning*](https://d2l.ai/) (free online, with
  runnable code).
- Kuhn and Silge,
  [*Tidy Modeling with R*](https://www.tmwr.org/) (free online), for
  the workflow in R: splitting data, tuning, and comparing models
  without fooling yourself.
- For ecology: Pichler and Hartig (2023,
  ["Machine learning and deep learning: a review for ecologists"](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.14061),
  *Methods in Ecology and Evolution* 14: 994-1016); Christin,
  Hervet, and Lecomte (2019,
  ["Applications for deep learning in ecology"](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13256),
  *Methods in Ecology and Evolution* 10: 1632-1644); Tuia et al.
  (2022,
  ["Perspectives in machine learning for wildlife conservation"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-27980-y),
  *Nature Communications* 13: 792).

## Discussion {#discussion}

> **Discussion:** A state agency has 12 years of lek counts at 400
> leks and 40 candidate covariates. A boosted tree model predicts
> held-out years with an $R^2$ of 0.71; a spatiotemporal GLMM with
> five covariates chosen in advance reaches 0.58. The agency has two
> uses in mind: mapping where to survey next spring, and deciding
> whether to restrict grazing near leks. Which model would you hand
> them for each, and what would you tell them about the other?

```{asis, echo=FALSE}
*Land:* Survey map: the boosted model (a prediction task, and it was
validated on held-out years, though ask whether whole leks were held
out too). Grazing decision: neither as is. It is a causal question;
the GLMM's grazing coefficient is closer to what is needed, but only
if the five covariates were chosen from a diagram and grazing was
not allocated in response to lek condition. The 0.13 gap in R2 says
nothing about which grazing estimate to trust.
```

> **Discussion:** Which one topic on this page would most change the
> analysis you are doing now, and what is the first hour of learning
> it going to look like?

```{asis, echo=FALSE}
*Land:* No right answer. Push for a concrete first step (a named
chapter, a toy data set to simulate), since "learn Bayesian
statistics" is not a plan.
```

## Bonus: other topics worth knowing about {#other}

Each of these is a field with its own books. One line and one
starting point apiece:

- **Models with imperfect detection** (occupancy, N-mixture,
  capture-recapture, distance sampling): the observation process is
  a second model stacked on the ecological one. Start with the
  [occupancy section](Week15_DynamicModels.html#occupancy) of the
  Week 15 page, then Kéry and Royle
  ([2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/C2013-0-19160-X)).
- **Integrated population models:** one likelihood for counts,
  survival, and reproduction data together, so each data set informs
  the others. Schaub and Kéry, *Integrated Population Models*
  (Academic Press, 2022).
- **Hidden Markov models** for animal movement and behavior:
  McClintock et al. (2020,
  ["Uncovering ecological state dynamics with hidden Markov models"](https://doi.org/10.1111/ele.13610),
  *Ecology Letters* 23: 1878-1903).
- **Time series and forecasting:** Hyndman and Athanasopoulos,
  [*Forecasting: Principles and Practice*](https://otexts.com/fpp3/)
  (free online).
- **Smooths and GAMs in depth:** Wood,
  [*Generalized Additive Models: An Introduction with R*](https://doi.org/10.1201/9781315370279)
  (2nd ed., 2017).
- **Missing data and measurement error:** treated as more unknowns
  to estimate, which a Bayesian model does naturally; see the
  chapter on both in *Statistical Rethinking*.
- **Learning with AI tools:** a language model is a patient tutor
  for all of the above, with the caveat this course has repeated.
  Ask it to explain, to quiz you, and to critique your model. Then
  check what it says by simulation: if you can simulate data from
  the model and recover the parameters with code you understand, the
  method is yours.
